newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end lower despite tame CPI data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end lower despite tame CPI data.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries shrugged off another tame inflation report and closed moderately lower on Tuesday, halting a three-day rally that market participants said may have gone a bit too far.

Late Tuesday, the 30-year bond was at 98-24/32, down 10/32. Its yield rose to 6.72 percent. Early in the session, the bond had fallen more than a half-point, but the somewhat cheaper levels enticed buying at the lows.
"The market is still overbought on a short-term basis," said a senior trader at a leading U.S. bank/dealer.

The market withstood an early bout of selling from hedge funds, foreign central banks and other accounts, as the market reverted to its recent trend of buying on dips. But the lack of follow through buying kept the market under pressure all session, players said.

Treasuries were weaker from the start and were unable to recover, despite a scant 0.1 percent rise in the May consumer price index. The CPI, along with the core rate, which rose 0.2 percent in May, were in line with expectations. Yet, traders said, the "good" news was already built into the market, and with Treasuries at the top of their ranges, rallying further proved difficult.

"The market is a little bit vulnerable at these levels," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc. "There is still cash to be invested, but you have to look beyond five-year notes to see value."

Analysts noted that two-year notes have hit a wall, and it is unlikely its yield will fall below 6 percent when it is not clear if the Federal Reserve will raise rates again. Twice in the past week the two-year note's yield has dipped to 5.99 but was not able to be sustained.
On Tuesday, it ended at 6.02 percent, up from 6.01 percent on Monday.
"To start doing better we will have to start talking ease," said a head trader at a primary dealership, adding that no one is talking about a Fed rate cut.
"So, the market is taking a rest here; they don't want to chase the market," he said. "It is fully priced, although we are a couple bad numbers away from correcting lower."
Players expect the yield curve to flatten, perhaps as much as another 10 basis points, as the long end likely leads the way in the near term.
"The market is pressed against fed funds probably going to 5.75 percent (from 5.5 percent)," the head trader said.
Meanwhile, a huge amount of corporate supply this week, estimated around $5 billion, helped to depress Treasuries on Tuesday, players said.
And, the selling of Treasuries for the new corporate issuance could be a factor on Wednesday.
The only item of interest on Wednesday is the Fed's Beige Book report on regional economic conditions. Economists said the market will be looking for signs of labor market tightnesss.

On Tuesday, not even weak data could spark the market. In addition to the friendly CPI, housing starts fell nearly 5 percent in May. But Treasuries fell a half-point, extending losses after the Fed said industrial production rose 0.4 percent in May.

The market also ignored remarks from San Francisco Fed President Robert Parry, who said the U.S. economy was performing "extraordinarily well." Parry, a Fed Board voting member, said economic strength is seen in all sectors and that despite tightness in labor and product markets, inflation is "quiescent."

As of 1500 EDT, trading volume was $76.9 billion, 15 percent above an average Tuesday in the second quarter, according to GovPX. Bill volume was 3 percent below average and coupon volume was 25 percent above normal.
Five-year notes fell 5/32 to 100-25/32 to yield 6.31 percent and the 10-year note was down 7/32 to 101-13/32 to yield 6.43 percent.
Three-month bill rates were up eight basis points at 4.92 percent, six-month rates were down one basis point t 5.10 percent and year bill rates were up one basis point at 5.34 percent.
(( -- North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
